name: Carabayo
sweep_summary: Carabayo (cara1245) is not in the catalog and cannot be: it is an uncontacted group whose entire linguistic record is ~55 word tokens written down by Capuchin missionaries in 1969. Both Glottolog 'prosody' items in the sweep (Alonso 1984, 1986, 'El Prosodion de Juan Gil de Zamora') are about a 13th-century Latin grammar treatise; the Glottolog reference pages show lgcode 'Carabayo [cby] (computerized assignment from \"gil\")', i.e. an automatic mis-tag on the word 'Gil' — irrelevant, priority none. The one real analysis, Seifart & Echeverri 2014 (PLoS ONE, open access, fetched sources and read,, says on p. 2 that acute accents appear on only four wordlist items, are not systematically marked, and are disregarded; it makes no claim about stress placement. The primary 1969 mission-bulletin sources (Juan Berchmans de Felanix 1969; Vidal y Pinell 1970) are print-only and low priority since the 2014 paper reproduces the whole corpus in its Table 1. Verdict: no stress statement exists for this language; keep it out of the catalog and drop the two mis-tagged Benjamins entries from its bibliography.

new_statements.quote: An acute accent appears in only four items (7, 9 = 18, 10, and 29 = 30). This suggests that whatever it may represent, it was not systematically marked. Therefore we disregard it for establishing hypothetical phoneme inventory.
new_statements.citation: Seifart, Frank & Echeverri, Juan Alvaro (2014). Evidence for the identification of Carabayo, the language of an uncontacted people of the Colombian Amazon, as belonging to the Tikuna-Yurí linguistic family. PLoS ONE 9(4): e94814. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0094814
new_statements.locator: p. 2, Materials and Methods, paragraph on transliteration of Juan Berchmans de Felanix's 1969 list (text file line 122-126); accent-marked items in Table 1, p. 3 (items 7, 9, 10, 18, 29, 30)
new_statements.reading: This is the only first-hand statement bearing on accent in Carabayo that exists in print, and it is a negative one: the whole attested corpus is ~55 word tokens transcribed in 1969 by a Catalan Capuchin missionary in Spanish orthography, acute accents appear on four items only (all, as it happens, on a final syllable: nauué, agó/pin-gó, amá, ané), and the only linguists to analyse the data treat the marking as unsystematic and set it aside. No word-stress placement can be coded for Carabayo from any source; the language should stay out of the catalog (or be recorded as 'no data'). The two Glottolog 'prosody' titles attached to cara1245 are a computerized mis-tag from the word 'Gil' (Juan Gil de Zamora's medieval Latin Prosodion) and should be dropped from the per-language bibliography.

sources.citation: Seifart, Frank & Echeverri, Juan Alvaro (2014). Evidence for the identification of Carabayo, the language of an uncontacted people of the Colombian Amazon, as belonging to the Tikuna-Yurí linguistic family. PLoS ONE 9(4): e94814.

sources.locator: p. 2, Materials and Methods (transliteration paragraph); Table 1 p. 3
sources.note: The only extant Carabayo data are ~55 word tokens (48 types) written down in 1969 by Capuchin missionaries (Juan Berchmans de Felanix 1969, Amanecer Amazónico XVI:5, 16-17; Venanci d'Arenys de Mar 1969) using Spanish orthography. The authors report that an acute accent appears on only four items of the list (7 ʔa-nauué 'give me, show me'; 9=18 agó / pin-gó 'bring'; 10 amá 'come'; 29=30 ané...), judge the marking unsystematic, and disregard it. No statement of where word stress falls is made; no tone or prosody is described. Observation (mine, not the authors'): all four marked accents happen…
